newsitem.title: GERMANY: IPO fever sweeps bullish German stock market. [CORRECTED 15:08 GMT]
newsitem.headline: IPO fever sweeps bullish German stock market. [CORRECTED 15:08 GMT]

text.p: The German stock market's greatest bull run ever has lured 12 German companies to list on the German bourse so far this year and investors are tripping over themselves to buy shares in the debutantes.
(Corrects from "12 German companies to list on DAX index").

The DAX has risen 46 percent so far this year and is, crucially, seeing unprecedented levels of liquidity. This has prompted more than 20 other German firms to plan Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) in 1997.

"There is no doubt that the popularity of shares has increased, also among private investors, and this helps to make the stock market a more attractive option for companies," Mathias Haffner, analyst at BZW in Frankfurt, said.

Monday sees the next listing on the German stock exchange when German machinery group R Stahl comes to market. The bookbuilding range has been set at between 30 and 35 marks per share, with 2.4 million shares due to be issued.

The IPO of shares in German software group Mensch und Maschine AG (MUM) on Wednesday was massively oversubscribed. When MUM is officially listed on July 21, it will be the twelfth company to come to market in 1997.

Other recent high-profile listings include the German television network ProSieben AG, shares in which jumped 32 percent on their first day of trading last week with a traded volume of 2.7 million shares.
ProSieben's listing raised nearly 1.26 billion marks ($701.3 million) for the company, increasing its capital by 360 million marks to over 700 million marks.

Germans have traditionally favoured the safer fixed-income investment route but with interest rates at historically low levels and the stock market on such a roll at the moment, equities are very much in vogue.

The main initiative driving the current rush to go public was the massive 20-billion mark IPO of Deutsche Telekom, which has done wonders to increase the profile of shares and equity-backed funds in the German investment arena.
Further state sell-offs on the cards include the sale of Postbank, due at some stage in 1998, and the sale of the rest of the airline Lufthansa AG later this year.
Analysts broadly welcome the increasing number of flotations, but insist that the market needs large-scale IPOs, like Postbank and Lufthansa, if the trend is to continue.
"As long as there is no massive correction this trend (of IPOs) should continue, but it is important that there are some bigger ones like Pro Sieben and Postbank," Haffner said.
A key factor behind the current rash of IPOs has the been the success of the New Market.

This new exchange for growth stocks is modelled on New York's NASDAQ exchange and was set up in March by the bourse operators Deutsche Boerse AG with the aim of breathing new life into the cautious German investment world.
At least 20 companies are expected to list on the New Market in its first year of operation.
Other high profile flotations so far this year so far have been the mobile telecoms equipment group MobilCom in March and savings bank BHW Holding AG in April.

Funds composed of German equities have seen an increase in returns of up to 41.5 percent in the first six months of 1997. On a one year basis, the average rise in the value of German equity-backed funds was 44 percent, with the highest rate of increase 62 percent.
"The investment fund organisations are saying they have never seen so much liquidity around," Haffner said.

"The test of the viability of the whole thing is going to be when this bull market is broken. Then we will see if private investors hold on to their shares, or whether there is panic selling," Haffner said.
